extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in technology policy, regulators, policymakers, and advocacy groups
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and policy criteria for protecting the integrity of public comments in regulatory rulemakings (notice-and-comment), including detecting and deterring fraudulent, automated, or unauthorized submissions and ensuring accountability for those who submit comments on others' behalf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to consider public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies are required to take public comments into account while developing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that agencies' legal obligation to consider comments makes the integrity of submitted comments essential to proper rulemaking; gaming the system with fake comments distorts public opinion and compromises the process' integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of comments / prohibition on fabricated responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments submitted must be authentic and not fabricated; the New York AG found 18 million of 22 million comments were fake in the 2017 FCC net neutrality rulemaking, with lead generators fabricating responses using real consumer names without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Broadband for America paid to generate and submit millions of fake comments; fake submissions undermine the public record and should be identified and excluded. Detection of large-scale fabrication (e.g., repeated names, identical text, suspicious metadata) is implied as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent required for submitting comments on behalf of individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups (and their vendors) must ensure they have obtained consent from consumers before submitting comments on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AG's report found lead generators fabricated responses supposedly collected via prizes/giveaways; the recommendation explicitly states advocacy groups should verify and document consumer consent prior to submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical safeguards against automated bulk/unauthorized submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt technical safeguards to protect against unauthorized, automated bulk submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites automated mass-submission examples (a college student submitting 7.7 million comments via software) and recommends that agencies implement measures (rate-limiting, CAPTCHAs, verification systems, anomaly detection) to prevent or flag automated and bulk fraudulent inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for advocacy groups and vendors
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups and third-party vendors that submit comments on behalf of individuals should be held accountable for the authenticity of those submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AG recommended holding such parties accountable; concrete enforcement examples include lead generators (Fluent, React2Media, Opt-Intelligence) agreeing to a $4.4 million settlement and behavioral changes. Accountability can include investigations, civil penalties, settlements, and mandated practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen legal deterrents against deceptive comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers should strengthen laws to deter the submission of deceptive comments in rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report recommends legislative action as a complement to agency technical and administrative measures; stronger statutory penalties or clearer prohibitions on deceptive comment practices are proposed to reduce future abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and mitigate coordinated 'comment wars' and mass campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that high-profile regulatory changes can become arenas for coordinated, high-volume comment campaigns by advocacy or industry groups attempting to out-comment opponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames such coordinated campaigns as distorting public input; agencies should monitor for coordinated mass campaigns and develop policies to distinguish organized advocacy from fraudulent or deceptive submissions (e.g., disclosure of sponsorship, source tracking, weighting/flagging mass-submitted content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use investigations and remedies to restore integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: State or federal investigations can uncover fraudulent comment campaigns and lead to remedies (settlements, behavioral changes) that mitigate future abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York AG investigation identified millions of fake comments and produced a report recommending reforms; enforcement actions such as monetary settlements and mandated behavioral changes for vendors are cited as practical remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for improved transparency around sources of submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: While not detailed as a formal rule in the article, the recommendations imply a need for greater transparency about who is submitting and funding comment campaigns so agencies and the public can assess authenticity and potential influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AG noted limits in evidence about direct company knowledge of fraud; transparency measures (disclosure of sponsors/vendors, provenance of mass submissions) are a logical part of accountability and detection strategies referenced by the report and FCC commentary.
